Highlights:
The OpenUSD Validation framework provides a system to validate assets, verifying core rules, schema rules, and client-provided rules via plugins, to ensure assets are robust and interchangeable between different USD workflows.

UsdValidationValidators are used to run validation tests. A single UsdValidationValidator instance represents a single validation test that can result in zero or more named validation errors when run. For example a "usdValidation:CompositionErrorTest" validator might test for multiple types of composition errors, returning errors for any composition issues it encounters.
...
Validator instances can be used to run validation tests, but more commonly a set of validators will be used, represented by a UsdValidationContext. A UsdValidationContext can be created from a vector of UsdValidators, which can be created manually, or obtained via metadata query methods on UsdValidationRegistry. UsdValidationContext also provides convenience constructors that determine which validators to use based on metadata filters, such as a list of keywords.
...
UsdValidationRegistry is the central registry that manages all registered validators. The registry is used to obtain validator instances via validator metadata (name, keywords, schemaTypes). The registry also provides access to registered UsdValidationValidatorSuites which represent predefined sets of validators (that can be used to create a UsdValidationContext). Finally, the registry can be used to register custom validators (see "Creating Custom Validators" below).
...
Validation tests can be run on a stage, layer, or prim, by using the various `Validate()` methods on UsdValidationValidator or UsdValidationContext. When validating using a UsdValidationContext, multiple UsdValidationValidator tests will be run in parallel.
...
Custom validators can be created either via the OpenUSD plugin infrastructure, which results in lazy loading of the validators, or via explicitly creating and registering validators via UsdValidationValidator and UsdValidationRegistry APIs.

A custom validator must implement a validator task function (UsdValidateLayerTaskFn, UsdValidateStageTaskFn, or UsdValidatePrimTaskFn) which gets passed to the registry during registration, and called when the validator's test is run. Validators should implement the task function at the appropriate granularity level. For example, if the validation logic can be succinctly defined to be applied to a prim, implement UsdValidatePrimTaskFn rather than UsdValidateStageTaskFn or UsdValidateLayerTaskFn. Using too broad a granularity can impact performance — for instance, a validator task that only needs to operate at the prim level but is implemented as a stage task may incur unnecessary stage traversal each time it runs.
...

The following example creates a UsdValidateStageTaskFn and UsdValidationValidatorMetadata to register an explicit validator.

| | Explicit | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metadata source | Caller provides `ValidatorMetadata` | `plugInfo.json` |

If other code needs to query your validator's metadata (keywords, schema types) before the validator is loaded, use plugin registration. If the validator is created dynamically or is only used by the code that creates it, explicit registration is simpler.

When validators or suites are registered via the explicit APIs (`RegisterValidator`, `RegisterValidatorSuite`) and not plugin registration APIs, the registry sends a `TfNotice`-based notification. Clients can subscribe to be notified when new validators become available. No notice is sent for plugin-based registration, since plugin metadata is already ... at registry initialization time.

- Plugin registration (`RegisterPluginLayerValidator`, `RegisterPluginStageValidator`, `RegisterPluginPrimValidator`) — the caller provides only the validator name as a `TfToken`. Metadata comes from the plugin's `plugInfo.json` and is parsed automatically during registry initialization.

...

1. Startup: `ValidationRegistry` parses `plugInfo.json` for all discovered plugins. Validator metadata (name, doc, keywords, schemaTypes) is available immediately, before any code is loaded.

The following key information will help you prepare for the new arrangements for business-to-business (B2B) parcel movements from Great Britain to Northern Ireland.
...
The UK Internal Market Scheme (UKIMS) enables eligible goods moving from a business in Great Britain to a business in Northern Ireland that are for sale to, or final use by, end consumers located in the UK to move without the need for a full international customs declaration and without incurring duty. 

All B2B parcels require information to be submitted onto the Customs Declaration Service (CDS). Your parcel carrier may submit this as part of their door-to-door service. This means that you have to provide some additional information to your parcel carrier, and in certain cases you may need to pay duty (such as goods destined for the EU), which you can reclaim if the goods stay in Northern Ireland (see section 5 below). You should check with your parcel carrier to understand their processes.
...
For goods sent to consumers in Northern Ireland for personal use, there are no individual customs declarations. There is no duty payable and you do not have to present goods to customs authorities. If you send goods to consumers your carrier will collect standard consumer data from you about the movement such as the recipient’s details and a description of the goods. You should check with your parcel carrier to understand their processes.
...
If your business sends goods in parcels from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, you’ll need to understand whether your customers are businesses or consumers. Different processes apply which could impact the information that your parcel carrier requires.
...
You will need to inform your carrier whether the parcels you are moving are going to a consumer or a business. You should discuss with your parcel carrier how they wish to be told this information. For example, some parcel carriers may require you to provide an identifier or agree a ‘standard operating procedure’. The arrangements may vary depending on the carrier, your business model and commercial arrangements.
...
Businesses sending or receiving B2B parcels can apply to be authorised under the UK Internal Market Scheme. This will mean that eligible goods moving from Great Britain to Northern Ireland which are for sale to, or final use by, end consumers located in the United Kingdom can move without the need for a full international customs declaration and without incurring duty. 

Your business can send the parcels from Great Britain to Northern Ireland using UKIMS if your goods meet the requirements of the scheme. You can find guidance on moving goods you bring into Northern Ireland as ‘not at risk’ of moving to the EU on GOV.UK
...
Either the sender or recipient of the goods can hold the UKIMS authorisation and use it to move B2B goods in parcels into Northern Ireland. If both the sender and recipient are authorised, it’s a commercial decision for these businesses to decide which UKIMS authorisation to use. You should consider if the sending or receiving business will act as the UKIMS authorised business and ‘importer of record’ and then inform your carrier.

If you do not currently hold a UKIMS authorisation, you should start to apply for this now. If you move goods under UKIMS, you will benefit from providing a reduced dataset compared to a full customs declaration.

As soon as you have obtained your UKIMS authorisation, you should tell your parcel carrier:

- your UKIMS authorisation number
- your Economic Operators Registration and Identification (EORI) number that is associated with your UKIMS authorisation
- when this should be used for parcels you send/receive (i.e. which movements are eligible to move under UKIMS)
- whether the sender’s or recipient’s UKIMS authorisation should be used (make clear which party is acting as the ‘importer of record’)

It is important that your parcel carrier knows who is acting as the ‘importer of record’ and therefore has legal responsibility for the accuracy of the data submitted to CDS.
...
. Moving goods using a UKIMS authorisation

When making parcel movements using the sender’s UKIMS authorisation, the sender:

- needs to confirm to their carrier that the goods meet the criteria to move as ‘not at risk’ under UKIMS - for some parcel carriers, this can be done once and held by the carrier within your account details
- should collect evidence to confirm this by obtaining confirmation from the recipient about whether the goods are for sale to, or final use by, end consumers located in the United Kingdom. This could be through knowledge they hold about their customers, through terms and conditions or other contractual arrangements
- should provide the carrier with their UKIMS authorisation number and the associated EORI number when arranging delivery, confirming to their carrier that the goods meet the criteria to move under UKIMS
- will need to keep evidence (as the UKIMS authorised trader) to support each ’not at risk’ movement into Northern Ireland and retain this for the 5-year retention period

When making parcel movements made using the recipient’s UKIMS authorisation, the recipient (receiving business):

- will need to confirm that the goods meet the UKIMS criteria
- should confirm to the sender that the goods are eligible to move under UKIMS (for example, senders may wish to set out in their terms and conditions that by providing a UKIMS number you confirm the goods meet the criteria)
- should provide their UKIMS authorisation number and the EORI number that is associated with their UKIMS authorisation to the sending business in Great Britain, or directly to the carrier based on the arrangements of your supply chain
- will (as the UKIMS authorised trader) need to keep evidence to support each ’not at risk’ movement into Northern Ireland and retain this for the 5-year retention period

If there is no UKIMS authorisation for the movement that can act as the ’importer of record’, or the goods are ‘at risk’ of entering the EU, then:

- the goods are not eligible and therefore cannot move under UKIMS, so you should inform your parcel carrier if there is no applicable UKIMS authorisation or if you require your parcel to be processed ‘at risk’ of entering the EU
- this means that full customs processes will apply, and duty may be due
- responsibility for completing customs processes and paying duty will depend on the terms agreed between carrier, seller and buyer
- there are a range of options available for sending parcels without paying duty if they are eligible
- you should tell your parcel carrier if you wish to claim a waiver or relief on the goods and check they will accept that process
- you may be able to claim for repayment of import duty paid, or remission of import duty deferred, if you pay duty on goods into Northern Ireland

The table below is how we translate each of those into something a tenant can enforce and an auditor can test. Your written configuration is a filled-in version of it.
...
| Review and approval for suitability before issue | Content approval switched on for the library plus an approval route per document type, so publishing is blocked until the named approver responds | For any revision: who approved it, when, and what they were sent — retrieved by filtering, not by searching three mailboxes |
...
| Retention and disposition of superseded revisions | Version limits chosen deliberately, retention or record labels where a revision must outlive them, and disposition review before anything is destroyed | The superseded issue an auditor names, plus evidence that nothing was disposed of without a recorded decision |
...
The mechanism is unglamorous. Content approval on the library gives you the gate: SharePoint supports requiring approval of submitted items and restricting who can see drafts, as Microsoft sets out in its guidance on enabling and configuring versioning for a list or library (opens in new tab). The routing sits on top of it: a flow using the Start and wait for an approval action, documented in Microsoft’s approval workflow documentation (opens in new tab), which supports a single approver, first-to-respond, everyone-must-approve, and stages in sequence for the procedures that need a technical reviewer before the quality manager.

What matters for an audit is the by-product. The approval decision, the approver, the timestamp and any comment are written back against the revision, which is the difference between an evidence request that takes thirty seconds and one that takes a morning. Two design notes worth stating because they decide whether the system survives staffing changes: the flow’s connections should be owned by a service account rather than a person who might leave, and every document type needs a named deputy approver, because a controlled set with one approver on vacation is a controlled set that people start bypassing.
...
This is the part most in-house builds get wrong, because the default behaviour is not the behaviour a quality system needs. A library version limit is a ceiling, not an archive: Microsoft’s documentation on version history limits for document libraries (opens in new tab) states that when versions exceed the limit set on a library, the versions matching the criteria are marked for permanent deletion, bypassing the recycle bin entirely. If the tenth revision of a procedure quietly evicts the first, the control procedure claiming you retain superseded issues is no longer true.
...
| A retention label that marks the revision as a record | Version deletion is blocked outright and a locked record cannot be edited — the strongest form of protection from unintended alteration | Editing requires unlocking, which copies the prior revision into the site’s Preservation Hold library; it needs Purview licensing and a taxonomy somebody maintains |
| Disposition review at the end of retention | Nothing is destroyed until a named reviewer approves it, and the decision itself is recorded as evidence | Reviewers need the disposition role granted deliberately, and the review queue becomes a recurring job on somebody’s desk |
...
Approvals, revisions and acknowledgements live in your own lists and libraries, so that history is yours for as long as you keep the items. The tenant-level activity record is different, and it is better to hear the constraint from us than from an auditor. Microsoft’s guidance on searching the unified audit log (opens in new tab) states that audit records are retained for 180 days under Audit (Standard), that Entra ID, Exchange and SharePoint activity is retained for one year by default for users with an E5 or equivalent license, and that a single search can span at most 180 days.

The practical consequence is a design rule rather than a problem: anything you must be able to evidence years later belongs in the library and its lists, captured as the work happens, not retrieved later from a tenant log that may have aged out. That is why the acknowledgement record is a list rather than a report, and why approval outcomes are written back onto the revision. We configure the audit log because it is useful for investigating a specific question — who changed that setting, when — not as the system of record for conformity.
...
Four things a normal library does not: a document cannot be published without the named approver signing it, staff see only the published revision, every superseded revision is retained rather than overwritten, and each document carries a review date that raises a task when it passes.
...
### Can we prove staff read the current revision? 

Yes, though SharePoint has no built-in acknowledgement feature, so it is built. A flow asks the named audience to confirm they have read a specific revision, and each confirmation is written to a list with the person, the revision number and the date, which exports for an auditor.
